sources.title: Women's Quest For Occupational Equality: The Case Of Jewish Female Agricultural Workers in Pre-State Israel

storyBeats: Ayanot was established near Ness Ziona in 1930 as a working farm for women, initiated by Ada Fishman Maimon.
WIZO’s Romanian Federation, the Women Workers’ Council, and the Pioneer Women of the General Workers Union supported the project.
The farm’s land was bought by the Jewish National Fund with a donation from Julius Schwartz.
Architect Richard Kauffmann designed the site, which opened in 1932.
Women worked across the farm: archival film descriptions record vegetable gardens, a nursery, a cabbage field, an orchard, a barn, and a poultry coop.
The work included practical tasks such as raising chicks, sorting eggs, harvesting, plowing, preparing food, and caring for the grounds.
Ayanot’s agricultural training covered branches beyond those commonly regarded as suitable for women, including work in citrus groves.
The working farm later became an agricultural school for girls; in 1952 it became a mixed agricultural school for boys and girls.
During World War II, the village received Jewish refugees from several countries.
During the 1948 War of Independence, the village served as a Palmach organizing and guarding point.

stories.brief: A 1966 documentary about Ashdod’s tenth anniversary recorded residents discussing the young city’s needs: Leyland workers described mass layoffs, a preschool teacher a budget shortfall, and a sports club a lack of training facilities, alongside the developing port and power station.

sources.title: Ashdod - Workers Tell About Their City | 1966

storyBeats: In 1966, the Histadrut produced a 14-minute documentary about Ashdod on the city’s tenth anniversary.
The documentary was directed by Natan Gross and photographed by Emil Knebel.
Residents spoke about the problems they faced in the young city, rather than presenting a simple celebration of its growth.
Workers at the Leyland Motors car factory described mass layoffs.
A preschool teacher said the school had too little budget money.
The local Hapoel sports association had to fight for places and equipment to train.
One resident described immigrants in the city as struggling to become a community.
The film set these local difficulties alongside a developing port and what it described as Israel’s largest power station.
The film’s closing perspective, attributed to local newspaper editor Nissim Yehezkel, was that a city cannot be built without problems.

stories.brief: Letters preserved in the Cairo Geniza reveal how Jewish women in medieval Egypt and the wider Mediterranean kept in touch with family living far away; one mother in 11th-century al-Raqqa asked her son in Old Cairo to write more often and send clothes and other items.

sources.title: Letter to Her Son, Dosa
Voices, Authorship, and Communication in Women's Letters from the Cairo Geniza
Women in Medieval Jewish Societies

storyBeats: A woman’s Judeo-Arabic letter to her son Dosa survives among documents from the Cairo Geniza; the letter is dated to the mid-11th century.
The mother lived in al-Raqqa, in what is now Syria, while Dosa was in Fustat, or Old Cairo.
She complained that she had written without receiving his reply and asked him to send letters more often so she could learn how he was doing.
She said that a letter from him felt like seeing his face and that news of her children mattered deeply to her.
She asked Dosa to tell her how long he would remain in Fustat and said she would be glad if he lived nearer to her.
The mother asked Dosa to persuade his brother to visit her and bring his children.
She requested money and particular goods, including a dark-blue head covering with white embroidery and worn shirts.
She also asked for antimony and other substances used for eye makeup or eye care; the letter’s editor notes that it is uncertain whether she might have been selling them.
The letter describes a family spread across different cities: the mother’s husband and sons were away, and she mentioned living with a daughter.
The surviving address and delivery notes name people involved in carrying or receiving the letter, including a carrier and his son.
The letter was probably dictated to a scribe or male relative, so it preserves the mother’s message without proving that she wrote the words herself.
Scholars describe distance and mobility as important reasons that women in medieval Jewish communities sent and received letters from family members.

stories.brief: Ayanot, founded near Ness Ziona in 1930 by Ada Maimon with WIZO support, began as a women’s farming village where residents worked in fields, gardens, a barn, kitchen, and poultry coop; it later became an agricultural school for girls and then for boys and girls.

sources.title: Ayanot Girls training farm | 1936
‘She’s Got A Man’s Head On Her Shoulders’ Ada Fishman (Maimon) as a Test Case For Women’s Political Activity

sources.publisher: The Israel Journal of Social Research
sources.title: Women's Quest For Occupational Equality: The Case Of Jewish Female Agricultural Workers in Pre-State Israel

storyBeats: Ayanot was established near Ness Ziona in 1930 as a working farm for women, initiated by Ada Fishman Maimon.
WIZO’s Romanian Federation, the Women Workers’ Council, and the Pioneer Women of the General Workers Union supported the project.
The farm’s land was bought by the Jewish National Fund with a donation from Julius Schwartz.
Architect Richard Kauffmann designed the site, which opened in 1932.
Women worked across the farm: archival film descriptions record vegetable gardens, a nursery, a cabbage field, an orchard, a barn, and a poultry coop.
The work included practical tasks such as raising chicks, sorting eggs, harvesting, plowing, preparing food, and caring for the grounds.
Ayanot’s agricultural training covered branches beyond those commonly regarded as suitable for women, including work in citrus groves.
The working farm later became an agricultural school for girls; in 1952 it became a mixed agricultural school for boys and girls.
During World War II, the village received Jewish refugees from several countries.
During the 1948 War of Independence, the village served as a Palmach organizing and guarding point.

stories.brief: A 1966 documentary about Ashdod’s tenth anniversary recorded residents discussing the young city’s needs: Leyland workers described mass layoffs, a preschool teacher a budget shortfall, and a sports club a lack of training facilities, alongside the developing port and power station.

sources.title: Ashdod - Workers Tell About Their City | 1966

storyBeats: In 1966, the Histadrut produced a 14-minute documentary about Ashdod on the city’s tenth anniversary.
The documentary was directed by Natan Gross and photographed by Emil Knebel.
Residents spoke about the problems they faced in the young city, rather than presenting a simple celebration of its growth.
Workers at the Leyland Motors car factory described mass layoffs.
A preschool teacher said the school had too little budget money.
The local Hapoel sports association had to fight for places and equipment to train.
One resident described immigrants in the city as struggling to become a community.
The film set these local difficulties alongside a developing port and what it described as Israel’s largest power station.
The film’s closing perspective, attributed to local newspaper editor Nissim Yehezkel, was that a city cannot be built without problems.

stories.brief: Letters preserved in the Cairo Geniza reveal how Jewish women in medieval Egypt and the wider Mediterranean kept in touch with family living far away; one mother in 11th-century al-Raqqa asked her son in Old Cairo to write more often and send clothes and other items.

sources.title: Letter to Her Son, Dosa
Voices, Authorship, and Communication in Women's Letters from the Cairo Geniza
Women in Medieval Jewish Societies

storyBeats: A woman’s Judeo-Arabic letter to her son Dosa survives among documents from the Cairo Geniza; the letter is dated to the mid-11th century.
The mother lived in al-Raqqa, in what is now Syria, while Dosa was in Fustat, or Old Cairo.
She complained that she had written without receiving his reply and asked him to send letters more often so she could learn how he was doing.
She said that a letter from him felt like seeing his face and that news of her children mattered deeply to her.
She asked Dosa to tell her how long he would remain in Fustat and said she would be glad if he lived nearer to her.
The mother asked Dosa to persuade his brother to visit her and bring his children.
She requested money and particular goods, including a dark-blue head covering with white embroidery and worn shirts.
She also asked for antimony and other substances used for eye makeup or eye care; the letter’s editor notes that it is uncertain whether she might have been selling them.
The letter describes a family spread across different cities: the mother’s husband and sons were away, and she mentioned living with a daughter.
The surviving address and delivery notes name people involved in carrying or receiving the letter, including a carrier and his son.
The letter was probably dictated to a scribe or male relative, so it preserves the mother’s message without proving that she wrote the words herself.
Scholars describe distance and mobility as important reasons that women in medieval Jewish communities sent and received letters from family members.
